topic.label: Sleep Homeostasis
topic.description: Sleep pressure, recovery, circadian interactions, and longitudinal regulation of NREM/REM sleep.

papers.title: Sleep Homeostasis Has Circaseptan and Circatrigintan Cycles Over Year-Long Timescales.
papers.abstract: Sleep homeostasis, the process by which sleep pressure accumulated during wakefulness is dissipated across non-rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, can be quantified as the nightly rate of decline in slow-wave activity (SWA; 0.5-4 Hz). Disruption of this homeostatic process has been documented in a range of neurological disorders including epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease and REM sleep behaviour disorder, yet its long-term dynamics in healthy individuals remain uncharacterized. The advent of subscalp EEG (sqEEG) platforms now makes continuous, naturalistic sleep recording feasible over months, enabling longitudinal study of sleep homeostasis at an unprecedented scale. Here we report the first such characterization in 20 healthy adults recorded continuously over 12-15 months. SWA slope was predominantly negative across all subjects, confirming intact homeostatic regulation and was stable across sex and age. Continuous wavelet transform analysis revealed significant circaseptan (~7-day) and circatrigintan (~28-day) rhythmicity in the majority of subjects, independent of sex. These findings establish a normative baseline for long-term sleep homeostatic dynamics and suggest that homeostatic sleep pressure dissipation is organized across multiple timescales beyond the single night, with direct relevance for neurological conditions in which this process is disrupted.

papers.title: Tau-driven hyperexcitability of locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons underlies sleep fragmentation and cognitive decline in mice.
papers.abstract: Early sleep disruption is a hallmark of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its underlying mechanisms are unclear. The locus coeruleus (LC) dopamine-β-hydroxylase noradrenergic (LCDBH) neurons are vulnerable to early tau pathology in AD. Using P301S transgenic mice and cell-type-specific tau overexpression models, we show that pathological tau accumulation selectively increases the intrinsic excitability of LCDBH neurons. Tau-induced neuronal hyperactivity disrupts sleep homeostasis, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and slow-wave activity, increases sleep fragmentation and microarousals, and delays both anesthetic induction and sleep onset. Furthermore, tau overexpression in LCDBH neurons leads to significant recognition memory deficits. Notably, optogenetic suppression of LCDBH-tau neuronal activity reverses sleep disturbances and rescues cognitive dysfunction. Our findings demonstrate that tau-driven hyperexcitability of LCDBH neurons is a core driver of early sleep and cognitive impairments in AD, providing a mechanistic insight and potential target for preclinical AD treatment.

papers.title: DPYD links glial lipids and myelination to sleep duration
papers.abstract: The regulation of sleep is heritable and conserved across species1,2, but the governing genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of DPYD--which encodes the pyrimidine catabolic enzyme, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase--in sleep. Using a cross-species approach, we show that DPYD and its orthologs act specifically in glia to promote sleep through the regulation of brain lipids. In mouse and zebrafish, we find that DPYD orthologs are enriched in oligodendrocyte lineage cells, and their loss reduces myelination and sleep independent of DPYDs established role in uracil catabolism to {beta}-alanine. Genetic and pharmacological manipulations of myelin in zebrafish show that altering myelination is sufficient to perturb sleep duration. In Drosophila, which lack myelin, we find that the DPYD ortholog acts in ensheathing glia to promote sleep through formation of glial lipid droplets, a proposed evolutionary precursor to myelin. Furthermore, a human GWAS-identified sleep variant2 resides in a conserved cis-regulatory element that selectively contacts the promoter of DPYD within oligodendrocytes, connecting the human genetic association to oligodendrocyte-specific control of DPYD. Together, these results identify a deeply conserved role for glial lipids in sleep regulation and establish DPYD as a mechanistic link between myelin biology and sleep.

papers.title: Standard touchscreen test procedures shift circadian rhythms in mice: a modified protocol to minimize circadian confounds
papers.abstract: Touchscreen based cognitive testing for rodents offers considerable experimental benefits, including a semi automated battery approach and the use of appetitive rather than aversive reinforcement. However, food reward and touchscreen illumination introduce potential confounds, as both food and light can shift, entrain, or disrupt circadian rhythms, which in turn can affect learning and memory. The potential for the test apparatus to impact endogenous circadian rhythms is particularly problematic when probing relationships between sleep, circadian disruption, and cognitive performance. After observing phase shifting of circadian rhythms in nocturnal mice tested using standard touchscreen test procedures, which include testing during the active period (early lights off), we evaluated the relative contributions of the illuminated screen and the appetitive food reward. Our results indicate that light emitted by the touchscreen chambers is responsible for the circadian phase shifting effects, with standard screen conditions inducing a ~3.5 h phase delay in daily activity rhythms when training is conducted early in the dark period for 7 consecutive days. We then modified lighting in the test environment and the home cage to identify parameters that would minimize circadian shifting without impairing visual discrimination or performance on a widely used cognitive test (Trial Unique Nonmatching to Location, TUNL). From the 10 conditions tested, we offer specific recommendations for modifying touchscreen test protocols to minimize circadian confounds, without impacting task acquisition or performance.

papers.title: Closed-loop acoustic stimulation promotes local slow oscillation train initiation and persistence in elderly adults
papers.abstract: Slow oscillations (SOs) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep support memory consolidation and metabolic waste clearance. Aging is associated with reduced SO amplitude and density and disrupted temporal organization, characterized by more isolated events and shorter SO trains. We investigated whether closed-loop acoustic stimulation (CLAS) could enhance the initiation and persistence of rhythmic SO activity in elderly adults. Twenty-seven participants underwent a baseline night followed by an experimental night, during which online-detected SOs were either stimulated using CLAS (STIM; n = 16) or left unstimulated (SHAM; n = 11). We quantified the proportions of isolated and consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and SO train length. Analyses assessed local effects around online-detected SOs and global effects across NREM sleep using offline detection. Locally, CLAS reduced the proportion of isolated SOs and increased the proportion of consecutive SOs, train-initiation probability, and mean train length. Global overnight effects were weaker but directionally consistent, primarily reflecting a shift toward longer SO trains. These changes occurred without a significant between-group difference in the change in SO density, and local effects remained significant after adjustment for SO density. Thus, CLAS promoted sustained rhythmic activity beyond changes in SO occurrence. These findings suggest that CLAS can modify the temporal organization of SOs in elderly adults, supporting its potential to mitigate age-related disruptions in SO dynamics. Temporal organization measures may complement conventional amplitude and density measures when evaluating CLAS effects. Further studies should establish whether these changes translate into cognitive benefits or improvements in other aspects of brain health.

papers.title: Thalamic stereo-EEG detects sleep stages N2 and N3 with discrimination approaching scalp EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep and epilepsy interact strongly during sleep stages N2 and N3, when synchronization of brain rhythms is increased. Sleep staging relies on scalp EEG, which is often absent or incomplete during stereo-EEG monitoring and unavailable from implanted devices, while thalamic leads are increasingly implanted for epilepsy neuromodulation. Given the role of the thalamus in spindle generation and slow oscillation dynamics, we hypothesized that thalamic channels would identify N2 and N3 (N2+N3) better than other intracranial sites. We analyzed 477 h of stereo-EEG with simultaneous scalp EEG from six adults, including 46 thalamic bipolar channels on 11 electrodes. Two classifiers were evaluated on identical channels: a random forest with hidden Markov decoding (RF + HMM) trained leave-one-participant-out, and the pretrained SleepSEEG algorithm developed without thalamic channels. The primary endpoint was discrimination of N2+N3 from other stages as classified from scalp EEG by a sleep expert. Among regions sampled in all participants, thalamic channels performed best (area under the curve [AUC] 0.94 with RF + HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG across whole recordings; 0.88 and 0.86 at night). With RF + HMM, thalamic channels outperformed mesial temporal and temporal neocortical channels in all six participants across whole recordings. The advantage persisted against channel-count-matched subsets and a white-matter control with both classifiers. Individual thalamic electrodes reached AUCs of 0.79-0.99 with RF + HMM (10 of 11 at least 0.89). These offline findings support thalamic N2+N3 detection and motivate real-time evaluation for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.

papers.title: AIM-STAGE: a self-supervised framework via adaptive interval-aware multi-kernel calibration and spectro-temporal exploration for few-shot EEG staging.
papers.abstract: Learning discriminative and generalizable representations fromelectroencephalography (EEG) signals with limited annotations remains a key challenge inautomatic sleep staging. Supervised deep models depend on large-scale expert labels, yetsleep annotation is costly and time-consuming. Existing self-supervised methods oftenunderuse EEG spectral-temporal structure and adopt fixed negative-sample strategies,which are poorly suited to the continuous transitions and ambiguous boundaries betweensleep stages. This study proposes AIM-STAGE, a self-supervised representation learningframework for limited-label EEG sleep staging. AIM-STAGE comprises threemodules. (1) Spectral-temporal exploration: maps EEG segments into the time-frequencydomain through the short-time Fourier transform (STFT), jointly extracting log-powerand cross-channel phase difference to characterize frequency-band activity and phasedynamics. (2) Local-global hybrid encoding: uses a CNN-Transformer encoder, in whichconvolutional residual modules capture local spectro-temporal patterns and a bottleneckTransformer models long-range dependencies. (3) Adaptive interval-aware multi-kernelcalibration: employs multiple Gaussian kernels and dynamic weighting to synthesizeinformative negative representations, improving view consistency and inter-sampleseparability. AIM-STAGE was evaluated on SLEEP-2013, SLEEP-2018,SHHS-D, and SHHS-H against ContraWR, DFformer, EEG2Rep, EEGPT, Superlet-MAE,and a supervised baseline across 1% to 15% labels. Accuracy improved from 88.67% to92.04% on SLEEP-2013, and AIM-STAGE outperformed all baselines on all four datasetswith higher kappa, macro-F1, and balanced accuracy, including on the pathologicalSHHS-D cohort. Ablation confirmed the contributions of the bottleneck Transformer,positional embeddings, physiology-informed augmentation, and calibration loss. Per-stageanalysis showed that N1 is the most difficult stage, with F1 ranging from 0.003 to 0.046,and adding EOG and EMG markedly improved its precision, recall, and F1. AIM-STAGE offers an interpretable and label-efficient self-supervised solution for EEGsleep staging, improving robustness and stage discriminability under scarce-labelconditions while reducing dependence on manual annotation.&#xD.

ai.summary: Proposes AIM-STAGE, a self-supervised framework combining STFT spectro-temporal features, CNN-Transformer encoding, and adaptive interval-aware multi-kernel calibration for few-shot EEG sleep staging. It outperformed six baselines across four datasets from 1% to 15% labels, raising accuracy from 88.67% to 92.04% on SLEEP-2013, with N1 remaining the hardest stage.

papers.title: Circadian multimodal physiological, ocular and behavioural data from a 40-hour forced-desynchrony protocol
papers.abstract: We present a multimodal dataset from twelve healthy adults (aged 19-30 years, 50% female) who completed a 40-hour ultra-short sleep-wake forced desynchrony protocol which scheduled 2 h 30 min of wakefulness in dim light and 1 h 15 min of sleep in darkness (2:1 wake:sleep ratio), with the protocol ending after the last wake period. This schedule compressed the typical 24-hour day into an ultradian 3 h 45 min cycle to decouple circadian and homeostatic influences on physiology and behaviour. During each wake interval, participants completed repeated assessments of visual psychophysics (chromatic temporal contrast sensitivity), pupillometry with silent-substitution stimuli, ocular structure (optical coherence tomography) and physiology (intraocular pressure), psychomotor vigilance, salivary hormones, and standardised questionnaires, alongside continuous actigraphy, electrocardiography, and recordings of core and peripheral temperature, blood pressure, and interstitial glucose. Two supplementary evening sessions under experimental light exposure and dim-light conditions provide comparison data on circadian phase (salivary melatonin concentration, dim-light melatonin onset). Data collected from one pilot participant and screenings of two excluded candidates are additionally included. This dataset supports reuse for investigating circadian dynamics across multiple domains beyond the retinal-function hypotheses of the original study.

papers.title: Anti-correlation time-frequency synergy and dual-granularity fusion for sleep stage classification.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep stage classification is crucial for diagnosing sleep disorders and evaluating sleep quality. Single-channel EEG sleep staging using central electrodes has garnered significant interest due to its ability to detect a higher number of sleep spindles and its cost-effectiveness. Nevertheless, several challenges remain, such as the neglect of interdependencies among features, reduced model sensitivity to the dispersion across features, potential information leakage during the learning of transition rules, and class imbalance. To address these challenges, this study specifically designs an automatic sleep staging network based on single-channel EEG. The network incorporates a multi-branch feature extraction module, which captures negatively correlated frequency features that exhibit significant variations during sleep transitions and promotes synergistic complementarity. Furthermore, a dual-granularity residual attention mechanism is employed to perform adaptive fusion along both temporal and channel dimensions based on statistical measures such as the mean and standard deviation. The causal transition-aware network ensures temporal consistency while facilitating effective learning of transition rules. The focal loss function is utilized to counteract class imbalance. Experiments on SleepEDF-20, SleepEDF-78 and SHHS datasets show that our method achieves the best performance with overall accuracy of 87.0%, 83.4% and 84.5%, respectively. For N1 stage classification which is more challenging, it reaches an accuracy of 57.5%, 52.5% and 49.3% on three datasets, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and its certain advantages over existing methods.

ai.summary: Designs a single-channel EEG sleep staging network using anti-correlated multi-branch frequency features, dual-granularity residual attention fusion, causal transition-aware learning, and focal loss. It reached overall accuracies of 87.0%, 83.4%, and 84.5% on SleepEDF-20, SleepEDF-78, and SHHS, with N1 accuracies of 57.5%, 52.5%, and 49.3%.

papers.title: A hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit for REM sleep-dependent consolidation of social memory
papers.abstract: REM sleep constitutes a critical window for memory consolidation, yet the brain circuits orchestrating this process remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify a lateral supramammillary nucleus (SuM)-medial septum (MS) projection as a REM sleep-specialized pathway essential for hippocampal memory consolidation. Fiber photometry and optrode recordings revealed that lateral SuM-MS projecting neurons were selectively active during REM sleep. REM-specific optogenetic silencing of this projection impaired consolidation of both social and contextual fear memories. Crucially, silencing of its downstream target, the MS-CA2 pathway, during REM sleep selectively disrupted social memory while sparing contextual fear memory. This functional dissection establishes a hypothalamo-septo-hippocampal circuit (lateral SuM-MS-CA2) dedicated to social memory processing, in parallel to the recently-described direct SuM-CA2 pathway. These results also position the SuM as a REM sleep-hub that routes information via parallel septal pathways to consolidate distinct memory modalities.

papers.title: Slow power-envelope associations among brain, heart, and gut signals during sleep: an exploratory multivariate transfer entropy study.
papers.abstract: Sleep and the brain-gut axis both involve the coordinated regulation of the central nervous system (CNS), autonomic nervous system (ANS), and enteric nervous system. Although the role of the brain-gut axis in sleep regulation is increasingly recognized, the dynamic information flow and its directionality among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep remain unclear as statistical associations. In this study, based on overnight sleep data from 24 healthy subjects, we simultaneously collected occipital electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram, and bowel sound signals, constructed a multimodal physiological signal analysis framework, and employed a multivariate transfer entropy method based on non-uniform embedding and k-nearest neighbor estimation to systematically quantify directed statistical associations at the level of slow power envelope co-modulations among the brain, heart, and gut systems within the framework of sleep staging. The results reveal a consistent pattern of directed statistical associations: information transfer from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeds that in the reverse directions across all sleep stages. Sleep-stage dynamics further dissociate within-system from inter-system information flow: internal information exchange within the brain and gut intensifies with sleep depth and weakens during REM, whereas inter-system pathways show divergent stage-dependent patterns: heart-to-brain flow increases from light to deep sleep, while heart-to-gut and brain-to-gut flow are suppressed during deep sleep. At the frequency-band level, the brain, heart, and gut each exhibit dynamically reorganized source-receiver roles across sleep stages, with specific frequency bands contributing differentially to each inter-system pathway depending on sleep stage. This study identifies exploratory statistical patterns of directional information flow among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep, providing hypothesis-generating observations for future studies on sleep and multi-organ interactions. These directed associations do not establish anatomical pathways, causal regulation, or clinical biomarkers, and should be regarded as exploratory.

Information flow from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeded reverse directions, with stage-dependent inter-system patterns such as suppressed heart-to-gut and brain-to-gut flow in deep sleep.

papers.title: Enhancing deep sleep with auditory stimulation to boost cognitive training responsiveness in people with Parkinson's disease and mild cognitive impairment: Rationale and design of the double-blind randomized controlled trial PD-CogT-Sleep
papers.abstract: Background: Cognitive training (CogT) is an established non-pharmacological intervention for people with Parkinson's disease (PD) and mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI). However, overall effects on cognitive outcomes are small to moderate and interindividually highly heterogeneous. Sleep -especially deep sleep- could be an important determinant of CogT responsiveness in PD, and may have beneficial effects on PD pathophysiology. Therefore, the enhancement of deep sleep by phase-targeted auditory stimulation (PTAS) could strengthen the effects of CogT on cognitive symptoms and counteract disease progression. Methods: PD-CogT-Sleep is a monocentric, partly decentralized, double-blind, randomized sham-controlled trial that combines two remotely delivered non-pharmacological interventions, to assess the additive effect of PTAS on digital CogT responsiveness in people with PD-MCI. The primary outcome is executive functions; Secondary and exploratory outcomes include further cognitive functions, participant-reported outcome measures, blood-based biomarkers, and high-density sleep electroencephalography markers. Outcomes are assessed at baseline, five weeks post-allocation and at 3-month follow-up. We aim to consecutively recruit N=50 participants, who will be randomized 1:1 to receive CogT+PTAS or CogT+Sham. Discussion: The PD-CogT-Sleep study integrates wearable and digital technologies to systematically combine a novel, non-invasive, sleep-enhancing intervention (PTAS) with established CogT to improve cognition and evaluate PTAS' disease-modifying potential through its effects on blood-based biomarkers in PD-MCI. The expected results will foster our understanding of the interplay of sleep, cognition, and neurodegeneration, and may guide further development of safe, feasible, scalable, patient-centered, technology-based non-pharmacological interventions counteracting cognitive decline in neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Psychomotor vigilance is multidimensional: evidence from index network analysis, parameter review, and neuroimaging.
papers.abstract: The Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT) is widely used to assess vigilance, with interpretation shaped by experimental parameters, index definitions, and neurophysiological context. This review examines stimulus modality, task duration, and interstimulus interval, then considers the calculation and use of PVT indices. An exploratory network analysis of 15 indices in 678 participants examines a three-group descriptive framework comprising Stable, Overall, and Control indices. Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging findings relate vigilance to waking oscillations, EEG network stability, preceding sleep physiology, and functional brain connectivity. Multimodal assessment offers opportunities to refine vigilance monitoring in sleep medicine, fatigue research, and occupational settings such as aviation and shift work.

papers.title: Dynamics of Sleep Architecture and Nocturnal Oxygen Saturation During Acclimatization at Intermediate Altitude: A Longitudinal Observational Study in Elite Athletes.
papers.abstract: Athletes typically undergo training camps living and sleeping at intermediate altitudes (1500-2500 m). Hypoxia reshapes sleep through central circuits regulating arousal, chemoreflex gain and sympathetic outflow. However, the relationship between peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and sleep architecture and how it co-evolves during acclimatization, is unclear. We tested whether SpO2 differs across sleep stages at intermediate altitude and whether its recovery is stage specific. Seventeen mogul-ski athletes (seven women) travelled from Montréal (Canada) to Tignes (France) for a 2-week altitude training camp (AltitudeCamp; 2100 m) in June 2025. During the first week (6 nights) and the last night of AltitudeCamp, athletes were provided with a validated ring pulse oximeter and an electroencephalography (EEG) headband. We evaluated the changes in sleep stage distribution across successive nights, scored on 30-second epochs and synchronized with oximetry data. Model estimates are reported as mean ± Standard Error (SE), raw data as mean ± Standard Deviation (SD). Average total sleep time was 429 ± 47 min (mean ± SD) and did not change during AltitudeCamp (p = 0.939). Across the first week, %N3 decreased logarithmically (β = -2.35 ± 0.72%/ln (night), p = 0.002) and %Rapid eye movement sleep (REM) increased logarithmically (β = 3.13 ± 0.88%/ln (night), p < 0.001), with no changes in %Wake, %N1, or %N2. SpO2 was lower during AltitudeCamp (95.2 ± 0.3%) than measures obtained in normoxia (98 ± 0.4%; p < 0.001), and overnight heart rate (HR) was 7 ± 2 beats per minute (bpm) higher than the habitual 58 ± 3 bpm observed in normoxia (p = 0.005). Wake SpO2 increased by 0.13 ± 0.01 percentage points per night (p < 0.001), with faster recovery in N1 (0.19 ± 0.02 percentage points/night; p = 0.006) and REM (0.23 ± 0.01 percentage points/night; p < 0.001), while N2 and N3 did not differ from Wake. HR declined by 0.79 bpm/night during Wake, similar to N3 (p = 0.26), but larger than the decline in N1 (p = 0.024) and REM (p < 0.001). In N2, HR did not evolve during the first week at altitude. At intermediate altitude, nocturnal SpO2 and HR show sleep-stage-specific dynamics that mirror central ventilatory and autonomic adaptation to hypoxia. Our data suggest that acclimatization is not uniform across sleep stages, and that the first 2 nights after ascent may capture the most rapid adjustments despite similar total sleep duration. Sleep therefore offers a heterogeneous and ecologically valid index of central nervous system (CNS) acclimatization, which can be monitored longitudinally with wearable EEG-oximetry.

ai.summary: In 17 elite mogul-ski athletes undergoing a 2-week camp at 2100 m, wearable EEG-oximetry showed total sleep time was unchanged but %N3 declined and %REM rose logarithmically across the first week, while SpO2 was lower and overnight heart rate higher than in normoxia, with SpO2 recovery occurring fastest in N1 and REM and slowest in N2/N3. The authors conclude that acclimatization dynamics are sleep-stage-specific and that the first two nights capture the most rapid adjustments.

papers.title: Photoentrainment as Bayesian Inference: How the central circadian clock may weight and integrate the intensity and wavelength of natural light to estimate astronomical time
papers.abstract: Synchronising with the Earth's 24-hour rotation using natural light as a timing cue presents a problem for the mammalian brain's central circadian clock. Natural light is highly variable and can take a range of values at any given time of day. For example, it fluctuates due to differences in weather conditions and across seasons. Therefore, an absolute value of light provides an uncertain indication of the time of day. Despite this uncertainty, the central clock maintains close alignment with astronomical time, and here we describe how this may be achieved computationally. We present a Bayesian model in which the clock's endogenous oscillation is used to predict the probability of observing features of light, including intensity and spectral composition, and their co-occurrence given the time of day. These predictions are drawn from a distribution of values typically experienced. When observed light falls outside the predicted range, a prediction error provides evidence that the clock may be misaligned with astronomical time. How much the clock adjusts its phase depends on the relative uncertainty associated with its internal prediction and observed light. These are combined as a weighted average according to their relative reliability, drawing the clock's updated phase towards whichever provides the more reliable estimate of astronomical time. Using natural light measurements collected over one week from 59 human observers and 100 days of environmental spectral measurements, we characterize how the variability of natural light systematically changes across the day and show how the clock may exploit this structure for circadian timekeeping. The model explains how the canonical shape of the phase response curve emerges from the relationship between light distributions and time of day, and how properties of light, including intensity and spectral composition, can be integrated according to their reliability. The central clock's synchrony to light may represent a specific instance of a general computational strategy employed by the mammalian nervous system, whereby sensory information is interpreted relative to an internally generated prediction.

ai.summary: Presents a Bayesian model in which the central circadian clock predicts distributions of light intensity and spectral composition given time of day and adjusts phase according to prediction error weighted by relative reliability. Using natural light data from 59 human observers and 100 days of spectral measurements, shows how light variability across the day can generate the canonical phase response curve shape.

papers.title: Poor Test-Retest Stability of Nocturnal REM Sleep Onset Markers in Narcolepsy Type 1.
papers.abstract: To assess the test-retest stability of nocturnal sleep-onset REM periods (nSOREMPs) in untreated patients with narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), and of nocturnal direct REM (nDREM) transitions and their clinical and biological correlates. We included consecutive children and adults with NT1 diagnosed according to ICSD-3-TR criteria based on excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) findings, or CSF hypocretin-1 deficiency, without using nSOREMPs for diagnosis. All patients underwent two untreated overnight polysomnographic (PSG). nSOREMP was defined as REM sleep within 15 minutes of sleep onset, and nDREM as direct transition from wakefulness or N1 to REM sleep without intervening N2 or N3 sleep. Among 227 patients (108 males; mean age 31.6 years (SD=14.8)), nSOREMPs were present on both PSGs in 41.8%, on one only in 35.7%, and absent on both in 22.4%, yielding poor test-retest agreement (κ=0.26, 95% CI 0.14-0.39, McNemar test p=0.10). Persistent nSOREMPs were associated with younger age, shorter sleep latency, more SOREMPs on the MSLT, and lower hypocretin levels, but not with PSG interval, symptom severity, or medication history. nDREM was present on both PSGs in 15.9%, on one PSG in 37.4%, and absent on both in 46.7%, with poor stability and persistence associated with younger age, shorter MSLT sleep latency, and lower CSF hypocretin levels. nSOREMPs and nDREMs showed limited test-retest stability in untreated children and adults with NT1. papers.title: Transient Alerting Effects of Karolinska Sleepiness Scale Ratings on Physiological and Driving Performance Indicators.
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine whether subjectively rating sleepiness on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS) gives rise to an alerting effect and, if so, how long it persists. Data from five driving simulator studies involving 83 participants were pooled. Time-locked trajectories of blink duration, blink closing velocity, heart rate, electroencephalographic (EEG) parietal α and frontal θ power, and lateral lane position variability were analysed around each KSS rating using linear mixed-effects models with condition-specific KSS baselines, a transient post-rating component, a late post-rating offset, and time-on-task terms. Immediately after the rating, several indicators shifted in an alerting direction: blink duration and standard deviation of lateral position (SDLP) decreased, blink closing velocity and heart rate increased, and parietal α power generally decreased. Frontal θ showed a more condition-dependent response. The estimated duration of the transient component was indicator dependent, ranging from 40 s for heart rate to the upper bound of the 120-s analysis window for SDLP. These findings have practical implications for driver sleepiness detection system development, validation protocols, and type-approval processes that rely on KSS as a reference measure. If ratings themselves are associated with short-lived physiological or behavioural changes, the timing and modality of KSS administration become important for ensuring valid ground truth labels. Future studies with control conditions, randomized or jittered rating times, and real-road data are needed to determine whether the rating-associated changes are causal and generalisable.

The development of artificial intelligence-based automated sleep staging programs can alleviate barriers to scoring by improving efficiency and achieving standardized results. However, careful implementation of these programs is needed to ensure appropriate use. Artificial intelligence models can generate unreliable clinical results if models are not trained on heterogenous data that represent both common and infrequent sleep disorders. It is essential to recognize the limitations of artificial intelligence-based scoring prior to integration in clinical workflows to promote meaningful improvements in care delivery.

papers.title: How Circadian Rhythms Shape Emotional Reactivity and Regulation: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms exert a profound influence on human physiology and behaviour, providing temporal organisation to sleep-wake patterns, cognitive performance, and affective functioning. Increasing evidence indicates that misalignment between internal biological clocks and external environmental or social demands critically affects emotional health. This narrative review focuses on the role of circadian rhythms in shaping emotional reactivity and regulation, with particular attention to chronotype, social jet lag (SJL) and shift work. Evening chronotypes show greater vulnerability to negative affect, difficulties in emotion regulation and a higher incidence of psychiatric symptoms compared to morning types, who typically display greater emotional stability. SJL, prevalent during adolescence, has been associated with mood disturbances, anxiety and impaired regulatory capacities, with screen exposure and late-night activities acting as aggravating factors. Similarly, shift workers frequently experience circadian desynchronisation, which disrupts executive functions essential for adaptive emotion regulation and predisposes them to stress, irritability and long-term mental health problems. Although these findings underline the strong relationship between circadian misalignment and emotional dysfunction, inconsistencies in results highlight the need for methodological refinement. Future studies should combine subjective reports with physiological markers and adopt longitudinal designs to track long-term trajectories; controlled light exposure, structured sleep-wake routines and organisational policies for shift scheduling, may represent promising avenues to strengthen resilience. By elucidating the mechanisms through which circadian rhythms modulate emotions, research can contribute to improving prevention and treatment strategies for mood and anxiety disorders, ultimately enhancing psychological well-being.

papers.title: Distinct Systemic Metabolic Remodeling and Neurobehavioral Deterioration in Chemotherapy-Treated Lung Cancer Models.
papers.abstract: Peripheral tumors and chemotherapy reshape host physiology, yet model selection for cancer-related neurobehavioral deterioration often remains empirical. In lung cancer, this deterioration often presents clinically as a somatic-psychological symptom cluster that includes fatigue, pain-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, and distress. We asked whether chemotherapy-treated subcutaneous and orthotopic Lewis lung carcinoma models reproduce a comparable symptom-related state or instead reflect distinct systemic and neurobehavioral contexts. Male C57BL/6J mice bearing subcutaneous tumors (STCG) or orthotopic tumors (OTCG), together with normal controls, were followed through chemotherapy using behavioral measures of fatigue-related performance, pain/discomfort responses, sleep-related responses, center-zone exploration and passive coping. These trajectories were interpreted alongside plasma metabolic profiles and targeted peripheral and brain pathological readouts. The two models diverged. STCG preserved survival and showed an active sickness-like pattern, including impaired rotarod performance, delayed sleep onset and a trend toward shortened thermal response latency. OTCG showed survival attrition, late-stage systemic deterioration, reduced thermal nociceptive responsiveness, prolonged pentobarbital-induced sleep duration and stronger behavioral suppression. Plasma metabolomics revealed broader remodeling in OTCG, involving ketone body, glutathione, one-carbon and redox-related pathways. Both tumor-bearing models showed peripheral oxidative stress and brain alterations involving Claudin-5, glial activation and synaptic markers. Exploratory within-model networks identified fatigue-related performance as a highly connected node, with differing behavioral and biological associations. These findings suggest that the two models capture complementary but non-interchangeable metabolic and neurobehavioral states under the tested chemotherapy conditions.

papers.title: A single day of natural daylight exposure and physical activity does not conclusively change circadian phase: A Bayesian crossover experiment
papers.abstract: Among the environmental signals that shape human physiology, the daily light-dark cycle is the primary zeitgeber of the human circadian system. Physical activity may provide an additional non-photic time cue and frequently co-occurs with daylight in everyday life. However, their independent and combined effects on circadian phase have rarely been disentangled under naturalistic daylight conditions. In a counterbalanced mixed-design experiment, 41 healthy adults (24 women; mean age = 23.7 years, SD = 4.3) participated in up to three 40-h visits on fixed individual sleep-wake schedules. Each visit comprised an 8-h exposure beginning 1.5 h after wake to natural daylight, daylight attenuated by amber-tinted glasses, or indoor electric light (within subjects; mean photopic illuminances: 1196, 460, and 75 lx), with otherwise dim-light conditions. Participants hiked for approximately 4 h or remained sedentary (between subjects; activity indexed by median heart rate reserve [HRR]; group means: 32.7% and 2.7%). Bayesian hierarchical models used individual photopic illuminance (ActTrust 2) and median HRR to predict change in dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO; primary outcome) and exploratory outcomes (daytime and evening sleepiness, mood, and wellbeing, daytime perceived exertion, and evening psychomotor vigilance). Per standard-deviation increase in log-transformed illuminance and median HRR, estimated DLMO changes were -4.22 min (95% HDI [-10.93, 2.22]; BF = 0.70) and -6.48 min (95% HDI [-13.79, 1.27], BF = 1.56), respectively. Evidence remained inconclusive for both predictors and their interaction. Exploratory findings were largely inconclusive, practically negligible, or favoured the absence of effects. The circadian effects of a single day of natural daylight exposure, with or without physical activity, therefore remain unclear. Resolving this question may require larger samples and brighter, repeated, or habitual exposure timed to phases of greater circadian light sensitivity.

papers.title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
papers.abstract: Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout. Before and after each period, 5 min of eyes-open resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) were obtained from a subset of 18 participants (8 female). Functional connectivity was calculated across 16 electrode-pairs in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Beta-band connectivity between the right frontal and right inferior-parietal electrodes increased following CBD (P = 0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected P [pFDR] = 0.022), and alpha connectivity showed an increase that did not remain following FDR correction (P = 0.036, pFDR = 0.428). No significant differences were observed following placebo for any frequency band (pFDR > 0.69). Replication in larger samples is needed to confirm generalizability and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Tick tock: how the body's circadian clock keeps cardiometabolic rhythm in check.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates the internal timing of numerous physiological processes through an approximately 24-h cycle. It comprises a hypothalamic central clock, which responds to light cues and entrains peripheral clocks within individual cells and organs that, depending on the tissue, regulate gene expression across diverse biological functions in a tissue-specific manner. Peripheral clocks are also entrained by feeding and exercise-related cues, enabling their synchronization with feeding rhythm and physiology. Together, these clocks maintain a complex molecular network essential for metabolic homeostasis. Disruption of circadian rhythms, driven by genetic, environmental, or behavioral factors, is increasingly recognized as a major contributor to cardiometabolic disorders. Modern lifestyles, including shift work, irregular sleep, prolonged exposure to artificial light at night, jet lag, and erratic eating schedules, misalign circadian clocks with environmental cues, contributing to disruption of circadian rhythms or chronodisruption. This misalignment alters hormonal regulation, promotes systemic inflammation, and impairs metabolic balance, thereby increasing the risk of cardiovascular disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related complications. The present review examines the mechanistic roles of core circadian clock genes in cardiometabolic health, highlighting their regulation of physiological processes in peripheral organs such as the heart, liver, and adipose tissue. We further discuss how circadian clock disruption accelerates disease onset and progression and explore emerging therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological modulation of the molecular circadian clock components and personalized chronotherapy. These approaches offer promising avenues to restore circadian alignment and mitigate cardiometabolic risk.

papers.title: Augmented cardiac growth hormone signaling in circadian-disrupted cardiomyopathy.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption, including rotating shift work, social jet lag, and chronic sleep disturbance, is associated with increased cardiovascular risk and may promote cardiac remodeling. The molecular mechanisms connecting clock disruption to structural heart disease remain incompletely defined. This minireview advances the hypothesis that the growth hormone, GH, axis is an underrecognized endocrine mediator. GH secretion is time dependent, with most daily secretion occurring during early nocturnal sleep-in humans. Cardiomyocytes express GH receptors, and GH can activate Janus kinase 2, signal transducer and activator of transcription 5, phosphoinositide 3 kinase and Akt, and mitogen activated protein kinase and extracellular signal regulated kinase pathways that influence cardiac growth and metabolism. We propose that the cardiomyocyte molecular clock restricts GH responsiveness to circadian phases. REV ERBα is a plausible component of this restraint, but direct cardiomyocyte evidence is lacking. Circadian disruption may increase or mistime myocardial GH signaling, promoting hypertrophy, fibrosis, and metabolic inflexibility. The strongest support comes from cardiomyocyte specific Bmal1 deficient mice, which show increased GH induced cardiac STAT5 phosphorylation, increased cardiac Igf1 expression, and remodeling. Reduction of GH receptor gene dosage partially attenuates this phenotype, supporting a causal contribution of cardiac GH signaling. Nevertheless, genetic clock ablation is not equivalent to environmental circadian misalignment in shift work or chronic sleep disruption. We critically evaluate the components of this proposed clock-GH-heart axis, identify unresolved questions, and outline experiments and chronopharmacological strategies to test whether restoring temporal control of GH signaling can prevent pathological remodeling while preserving physiological GH action.

papers.title: Multiscale Neurodynamic Alterations in Major Depressive Disorder Revealed by Lempel-Ziv Complexity of Multi-Paradigm Resting-State EEG.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) abnormalities in major depressive disorder (MDD) have predominantly been examined through single-frequency band analyses or single-scale nonlinear measures, and largely within a single resting-state paradigm, which limits the characterization of regulatory interactions across temporal scales. In this study, we investigated dynamic transitions and integrative patterns of multiscale EEG activity in MDD across multiple resting-state paradigms, with a focus on characterizing alterations in multiscale neural dynamic organization. Based on multiscale Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC), we derived two classes of features quantifying the Scale-Dependent Variation Slope and the Cross-Scale Correlation Coefficient. Resting-state EEG from the MDD Patients and Healthy Controls EEG Data (MPHC) was analyzed under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions to compare multiscale regulatory dynamics between patients with MDD and healthy controls. Patients with MDD showed impaired complexity transitions from low to high frequencies and disrupted delta-centered cross-scale integration. Distinct coupling reconfiguration patterns emerged across resting states, indicating a systemic imbalance in multiscale integrative organization. Classification models built from statistically selected features performed consistently across Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbor, and Decision Tree algorithms, reaching a maximum accuracy of 85.71% with a balanced sensitivity-specificity profile. Convergent results across models further suggested the preliminary discriminative value of the proposed features within the present dataset. These findings provide a preliminary multiscale neurodynamic framework for EEG characterization in MDD and suggest that cross-scale integration differences may provide a quantitative basis for characterizing multiscale EEG dynamics in depression.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Graph Analysis Reveals Enhanced Alpha-Band Integration in High-IQ Individuals: The MENSA-Connect Project.
papers.abstract: To assess whether resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) connectivity differs between high-intelligence individuals (MENSA members) and controls using graph-theory metrics: clustering coefficient, characteristic path length, and small-worldness. Resting-state 64-channel EEG data were recorded in 29 MENSA participants and 20 controls. Functional connectivity was estimated using Lagged Linear Coherence across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Graph-theory measures were computed using sLORETA and the Brain Connectivity Toolbox. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test; p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Compared with controls, MENSA participants showed significantly lower characteristic path length in the alpha band (Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) critical value = 0.004), indicating greater global network integration. In the beta band, they showed a higher clustering coefficient (BH critical value = 0.008), reflecting greater local specialization; together with a higher characteristic path length (BH critical value = 0.013), suggesting reduced global communication. No significant group differences were observed in small-worldness across frequency bands. High-Intelligence Quotient (IQ) individuals show a frequency-dependent resting-state cortical organization, characterized by enhanced alpha-band integration and increased beta-band local specialization. These findings support a nuanced neural-efficiency model of intelligence without changes in small-world architecture. Given the cross-sectional and observational design, these findings should be regarded as associative rather than causal and require replication in larger, independent samples. These findings indicate frequency-specific differences in functional network organization, although their cognitive implications remain to be established.

papers.title: In-person UCLA-PEERS® program for adolescents with autism spectrum disorder in Italy: study protocol for a pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial with pragmatic features and exploratory EEG markers of treatment response.
papers.abstract: Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Level 1 frequently experience persistent difficulties in peer relationships and social functioning that become more evident as social demands increase. Group-based social skills trainings represent a key evidence-based intervention for this population, yet its availability in routine clinical services is still limited. The Program for the Education and Enrichment of Relational Skills (PEERS®) is one of the most empirically supported interventions for autistic adolescents. In Italy, telemedicine delivery has shown promising results, but the effectiveness and implementation of the in-person format in real-world services have not yet been evaluated. In addition, predictors of individual response to psychosocial interventions remain largely unknown. This study is designed as a two-arm pilot and feasibility randomized controlled trial incorporating pragmatic features, including delivery within a routine tertiary clinical service, comparison with Treatment as Usual (TAU), and allowance for ongoing concomitant clinical, educational, and pharmacological treatments. It will compare the in-person Italian adaptation of UCLA PEERS® with Treatment as Usual (TAU) at IRCCS Fondazione Stella Maris (Pisa, Italy). Thirty-six adolescents aged 11-13 years with ASD (DSM-5-TR) and Full-Scale IQ >85 will be assessed at baseline (T0) and after the 16-week intervention (T1). Randomization will use block allocation with allocation concealment until completion of baseline assessments; outcome assessors and independent ADOS-BOSCC video coders will remain blind to group assignment. The intervention includes sixteen weekly 90-minute group sessions delivered by certified providers, with parallel caregiver sessions and structured teacher contacts to promote generalization. The primary focus of this pilot trial is feasibility, assessed through recruitment, retention, session attendance, and treatment fidelity. Clinical outcomes will be examined exploratorily to provide preliminary estimates of treatment effects. The QSQ-R will serve as the prespecified principal clinical outcome for estimating change in social functioning from baseline to T1. Parent- and adolescent-report versions will be analyzed separately, considering the Social Initiative and Social Reciprocity dimensions as distinct outcomes rather than deriving a composite total score. Key secondary outcomes include social knowledge (TASSK-R), autism-related social responsiveness (SRS-2), social motivation (SSDS), social anxiety (SAS), and observational change in social-communication behaviors (ADOS-BOSCC). Emotional-behavioral functioning (CBCL; YSR) will be explored as additional secondary outcomes. Baseline electroencephalography (EEG) recorded during a gesture-word integration task will be used to derive the N400 congruency effect and to explore whether individual differences in this measure are associated with treatment response. As a pilot and feasibility trial, the study is not powered for definitive efficacy testing and will estimate feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and preliminary effect sizes to inform future multicenter trials. This study will provide the first evaluation of in-person PEERS® in the Italian clinical context and test the generalizability of previous telemedicine findings in routine care. The integration of clinical and behavioral outcomes may contribute to mechanism-informed, personalized psychosocial interventions for autistic adolescents and guide the design of future confirmatory studies. papers.title: Immunometabolic reprogramming: a working framework for disease development, endotype differentiation, and therapeutic considerations in pediatric asthma.
papers.abstract: Paediatric asthma exhibits marked clinical heterogeneity and cannot be simply considered the childhood counterpart of adult asthma. Early-life environmental exposures can reshape immune-cell metabolic programs and potentially drive long-lasting inflammatory phenotypes. Existing explanatory frameworks for paediatric asthma largely centre on Th2-related inflammation, epithelial-alarm signalling and neuro-immune crosstalk, while the contributions of immunometabolic processes to disease endotypes remain under-summarised. This review collates available evidence regarding metabolic reprogramming in the pathogenesis of paediatric asthma and provides an integrated immunometabolic perspective on this condition. Summarized evidence covers immunometabolic changes across key airway-resident and infiltrating cell populations. Discussion addresses core paediatric-specific biological features, including early-life developmental windows, virus-related trained immunity, obese asthma, circadian-sleep interactions, neuro-metabolic-immune communication and metabolomics-based endotyping. The framework is organized around substrate competition rather than a glycolysis-versus-OXPHOS binary, because Tregs, M2-like macrophages and pathogenic ILC2s share lipid and amino-acid pools but exert opposing functions. From these observations emerges a testable "Metabolic Latching Model" of how early-life insults establish persistent inflammatory memory through metabolism-epigenetic coupling, with "latching" operationally defined by exposure removal and persistence beyond responding-cell turnover. Group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) and the Treg-to-effector balance are placed at the centre of this framework. Three hypotheses are prioritised as feasible with current technology: H1 (monocyte glycolytic baseline predicting wheeze-to-asthma transition), H4 (metabolic intervention in obese asthma), and H6 (the HDAC2-GSH/butyrate axis in steroid sensitivity). Current evidence suggests that immunometabolic reprogramming serves as one plausible contributing factor for the heterogeneity of paediatric asthma. This conceptual framework may bridge molecular metabolic findings and paediatric clinical contexts, and inform future mechanistic and clinical studies in this research area.

papers.title: Tirzepatide for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea: from apnea-hypopnea index reduction to cardiometabolic risk mitigation-a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic respiratory disorder with nocturnal oxygen desaturation that is often associated with multisystemic sequelae such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, and increased morbidity and mortality. Obesity has been proposed as a modifiable risk factor; hence, the recent shift in focus to investigating anti-obesity medications for the management of OSA. Tirzepatide is the first U.S. FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for the treatment of moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity to be utilized in combination with low caloric intake and physical activity, given its prior success in managing type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity. This narrative review evaluates tirzepatide and the SURMOUNT-OSA trial program as the key contemporary anchors for the pharmacological treatment of OSA in adults with concurrent obesity. Because the randomized evidence base currently comprises a single pivotal trial program, the review centers on SURMOUNT-OSA and its prespecified endpoints along with post hoc analyses, supplemented by observational, modeling, and mechanistic studies. In the SURMOUNT-OSA program, tirzepatide produced randomized, placebo-controlled reductions in the apnea-hypopnea index, sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, body weight, and systemic inflammation. The program was designed around respiratory and metabolic endpoints rather than clinical events, so it cannot support conclusions about mortality, cardiovascular, or renal outcomes. Favorable signals for those events, including all-cause mortality, major adverse kidney events, and major adverse cardiovascular events, come only from nonrandomized observational cohorts and are best regarded as directional and exploratory rather than definitive. Tirzepatide may help frame OSA as a multifactorial and partially metabolically treatable disease and may represent a clinically meaningful expansion of treatment options alongside, rather than as a replacement for, established mechanical and procedural therapies. The available evidence is anchored in a single phase 3 trial program and limited by short follow-up and the absence of definitive comparative and long-term outcome data. Long-term durability of effect after discontinuation, generalizability beyond the SURMOUNT-OSA-eligible population, OSA-specific economic analysis, and head-to-head comparisons against CPAP remain the principal unsettled questions requiring dedicated long-term studies before firm clinical recommendations can be made.

papers.title: Sphenoidal Meningioma with Focal Seizures Masquerading as Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome in HIV Patient.
papers.abstract: Seizures in adults with HIV can result from structural lesions, opportunistic infections, immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) or medication effects, making accurate diagnosis challenging. We report a 47-year-old woman with HIV who developed recurrent focal-onset seizures evolving to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures beginning approximately 4 weeks after initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Neurological examination was unremarkable. Electroencephalography revealed focal slowing over the left anterior temporal region without generalised epileptiform discharges. Targeted infectious testing, including Toxoplasma gondii , Cryptococcus neoformans and Mycobacterium tuberculosis , was negative. Brain magnetic resonance imaging performed at the time of evaluation demonstrated a well-circumscribed, extra-axial mass over the left sphenoid wing measuring 3.0 cm × 4.3 cm, isointense on T1-and T2-weighted sequences, with vasogenic oedema and midline shift, consistent with meningioma. Seizure control was achieved with antiseizure medication; however, definitive treatment required gross total surgical resection. Following surgery, the patient remained seizure-free at 12 months of follow-up. Although ART initiation initially suggested central nervous system IRIS, preserved immune function, negative infectious workup and characteristic imaging confirmed a structural aetiology. This case highlights the importance of a broad differential diagnosis and integrating clinical, electrophysiological, infectious and imaging data to identify treatable structural lesions in adults with HIV.
